cards.q: What does `sizeof(int*)` give in a 64-bit program, and why does it not depend on what the pointer points at?
cards.a:
8, because a pointer holds an address and every address in a 64-bit program takes 8 bytes

A pointer holds only an address, and in a 64-bit program every address is 8 bytes, whatever is stored there. The type lives in the compiler, not in the pointer's bytes.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Is a Row of Bytes

cards.q: Why do the addresses printed change every time the program runs?
cards.a:
Windows places the program, stack and heap at random positions each run (ASLR)

Address space layout randomisation moves the starting point each run. The layout inside, such as the distances between your variables, usually stays the same.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Is a Row of Bytes

cards.q: An int holding `0x0A0B0C0D` is stored at address `0x500` on a little-endian machine. What byte is at `0x500`?
cards.a:
`0x0D`, the least significant byte

Little-endian puts the least significant byte at the lowest address, so the bytes from `0x500` up are `0D 0C 0B 0A`.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Is a Row of Bytes

cards.q: Why must a `char*` be cast to `void*` before printing it with `std::cout`?
cards.a:
`std::cout` treats a `char*` as text and prints characters up to a zero byte

`std::cout` has a special overload that treats `char*` as the start of a C string. `void*` means "just an address" and prints in hexadecimal.
cards.lessonTitle: Memory Is a Row of Bytes

cards.q: `int* p{ &score };` What is the value stored in `p`, and what is the value of `&p`?
cards.a:
`p` holds `score`'s address; `&p` is the address of `p` itself, a different place in memory

A pointer is an ordinary variable with its own address. Its value is `score`'s address, and `&p` asks where the pointer itself lives.
cards.lessonTitle: Pointers Are Variables That Hold Addresses

cards.q: In `int* a, b;` what type is `b`?
cards.a:
A plain `int`, because the star applies to `a` only

The `*` belongs to the name it is written next to, so only `a` is a pointer. Write `int* a; int* b;` or `int *a, *b;` to get two pointers.
cards.lessonTitle: Pointers Are Variables That Hold Addresses

cards.q: Why will the compiler not let an `int*` hold the address of a `double`?
cards.a:
The pointer's type says how to read the bytes there, and reading a double's bytes as an int is meaningless

Both pointers are 8 bytes; the difference is what the compiler will do when you dereference. Converting between them needs an explicit cast, because it is almost always a mistake.
cards.lessonTitle: Pointers Are Variables That Hold Addresses

cards.a:
No, they are two different objects at two different addresses

Comparing addresses asks whether two pointers name the same object, not whether the values are equal. `a == b` is true, `&a == &b` is false.
cards.lessonTitle: Pointers Are Variables That Hold Addresses

cards.q: `int x{ 3 }; int* p{ &x }; *p = *p * 2;` What is `x`?
cards.a:
6, because `*p` is `x` itself

Dereferencing gives the object at the address, so `*p = *p * 2` reads `x` and writes `x`.

cards.q: What is the difference between `p->hp` and `*p.hp`?
cards.a:
`p->hp` means `(*p).hp`; `*p.hp` means `*(p.hp)`, which does not compile for a plain pointer

`.` binds tighter than `*`, so `*p.hp` tries to take member `hp` of the pointer itself. `->` follows the pointer and then takes the member.

cards.q: Which of these compile? `const int* a; *a = 1;` and `int* const b{ &x }; *b = 1;`
cards.a:
Only the second: `a` points at a const int, while `b` is a const pointer to a changeable int

`const` before the `*` protects the value pointed at; `const` after the `*` protects the pointer. `b` cannot be re-pointed, but `*b` can be written.

cards.q: Two pointers `p` and `q` hold the same address. `*p = 9;` What is `*q`?
cards.a:
9, because both reach the same object

Pointers holding the same address are two names for one object. A write through either is seen through the other.

cards.q: Why does `void heal(int h) { h += 25; }` not change the caller's variable?
cards.a:
The argument is copied into `h`; the function changes its copy, which disappears when it returns

C++ passes arguments by value. To change the caller's variable the function needs its address (a pointer) or a reference.

cards.q: `heal(int* h)` is called with `heal(&health)`. Is the pointer copied?
cards.a:
Yes, but the copy holds the same address, so `*h` reaches the caller's `health`

Every argument is copied, pointers included. A copy of an address still leads to the same object.

cards.q: When is a pointer parameter better than a reference parameter?
cards.a:
When "no object" is meaningful and the caller may pass `nullptr`, or for a C-style interface

A reference can also change the caller's object and is no slower. A pointer earns its place when null is a valid "not given", or when the interface must be callable from C.

cards.q: A function writes `*countOut = n;` and the documentation says `countOut` is optional. What is missing?
cards.a:
A null check: `if (countOut) *countOut = n;`

Optional means the caller may pass `nullptr`, and writing through `nullptr` crashes. Check before you write.

cards.q: A crash says "read access violation, `p` was `0x10`". What most likely happened?
cards.a:
`p` was `nullptr` and the code read a member at offset `0x10`

Reading `p->member` adds the member's offset to `p`. If `p` is null, the faulting address is just the offset, a tiny number like `0x10`.

cards.q: Why is a dangling pointer harder to find than a null pointer?
cards.a:
Its old memory often still works until reused, so the crash comes far from the bug

Following a null pointer faults at once. A dangling pointer still points at memory that is mapped and often holds the old value, so the bug shows up later, when something else reuses that memory.

cards.q: In an MSVC debug build a pointer shows the value `0xDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDD`. What does that tell you?
cards.a:
The pointer was read from freed heap memory: the object holding it was already deleted

The debug heap fills freed blocks with `0xDD`. A pointer full of `DD` bytes was loaded from an object that no longer exists.

cards.q: Why is keeping a pointer to `v[0]` across `v.push_back` risky?
cards.a:
`push_back` may move the elements and free the old block

When the capacity runs out, the vector allocates a bigger block, moves the elements and frees the old block. Any pointer into the old block then dangles.

cards.q: An array of `double` starts at `0x2000`. Where is element 3?
cards.a:
`0x2018`, because 0x2000 + 3 × 8 = 0x2000 + 24

Element i sits at the start plus i times the element size, and a `double` is 8 bytes. 24 in hexadecimal is `0x18`, not `0x24`.

cards.q: Inside `void f(int values[10])`, what is `sizeof(values)` on 64-bit Windows?
cards.a:
8, the size of a pointer

An array parameter is really a pointer: the array decayed and the 10 is ignored. `sizeof` measures the pointer.

cards.q: Why do C-style functions take a count alongside the array?
cards.a:
The function receives only the address of the first element, so the length is lost

When an array is passed it decays to a pointer to its first element. Nothing about its length travels with it, so the caller passes it separately.

cards.q: What does `values[i]` mean in terms of pointers?
cards.a:
`*(values + i)`: move `i` elements along from `values` and follow the address

Indexing is pointer arithmetic plus a dereference. `*values + i` adds to the value of element 0 instead, a common slip.

cards.q: `double* d` points at `0x1000`. What address is `d + 3`?
cards.a:
`0x1018`

Adding 3 to a `double*` moves three doubles of 8 bytes each: 24 bytes, which is `0x18`. The compiler multiplies by the element size for you.

cards.q: `int* a = &v[2]; int* b = &v[9];` What is `b - a`?
cards.a:
7 elements

Subtracting pointers into one array counts the elements between them, not the bytes: 9 - 2 = 7.

cards.q: Why is `end = begin + count` allowed but `*end` is not?
cards.a:
The one-past-the-end pointer may be computed and compared, but there is no element there to read

The language lets you form the address one past the last element so loops can stop at it. Dereferencing it reads memory that is not part of the array.

cards.q: You need the address 6 bytes after an `int* p`. How do you compute it?
cards.a:
`reinterpret_cast<unsigned char*>(p) + 6`

Arithmetic on an `int*` moves in 4-byte steps, so `p + 6` is 24 bytes on, and 6 is not a whole number of ints. Through a byte pointer, each step is one byte.

cards.q: How many bytes does the string literal `"pointer"` take?
cards.a:
8, seven characters and the terminating zero

A C string ends with a zero byte that is part of the literal, so `sizeof("pointer")` is 8.

cards.q: Why does a find function return `end` instead of `nullptr` for "not found"?
cards.a:
`end` is always a valid position to compare against, and the caller can search any sub-range the same way

`end` already marks "past the last element" for the range being searched, so "not found" needs no special value, and it works for a sub-range too, as in the standard library.

cards.q: What does `strcpy` do if the destination array is too small?
cards.a:
It keeps writing past the end of the destination until it has copied the source's zero byte

`strcpy` knows nothing about the destination's size. It copies up to and including the zero byte, overwriting whatever follows the array.

cards.q: A function stores `s.c_str()` from a `std::string` parameter passed by value. What is wrong?
cards.a:
The parameter is destroyed when the function returns, so the stored pointer dangles

A by-value parameter is a local copy. Its characters are freed when the function returns, so any pointer into them dangles.

cards.q: A grid is 10 wide and 6 high, stored row-major. What is the index of column 3, row 4?
cards.a:
43, because 4 × 10 + 3

Row-major means whole rows one after another, so index = y × width + x. Swapping x and y gives 34, the most common mix-up.

cards.q: An image is 100 pixels wide with a stride of 128 pixels. Where does pixel (0, 1) start, counted in pixels from the top-left?
cards.a:
At 128, one stride on

The stride is the real row length in memory, including any padding after the visible pixels. Each new row starts one stride further on.

cards.q: An image comes out slanted, each row shifted a little more than the last. What is the likely bug?
cards.a:
The code used the width where it needed the stride

Each row starts at the wrong place by the same amount, the padding, and the error builds up row by row, so the picture leans. Mixing bytes and pixels has the same effect.

cards.q: Why is a sub-view cheap?
cards.a:
It is a new start pointer and size that shares the memory

A sub-view is a new start pointer, width and height with the original stride, pointing into the original image's memory, so making one copies nothing. A change through the view changes the original.

cards.q: Why is `*reinterpret_cast<std::uint32_t*>(&someFloat)` wrong even though it usually prints the right bits?
cards.a:
It breaks strict aliasing, so the behaviour is undefined

Both types are 4 bytes, and the bits come out right in a debug build, which is what makes it tempting. The compiler may assume a `uint32_t*` never points at a `float`, so optimised builds may reorder or drop the read.

cards.q: Which types may legally view the bytes of any object?
cards.a:
`char`, `unsigned char` and `std::byte`

These three are the language's byte types. `void` cannot be dereferenced at all, and `bool` is not allowed to view arbitrary bytes.

cards.q: How do you read a 4-byte number stored at offset 6 of a byte buffer?
cards.a:
`std::memcpy(&value, buffer + 6, 4)`

Copy the bytes (or assemble them with shifts). A pointer cast is an aliasing violation and a misaligned read, and `+ 6` after the cast moves 24 bytes. `buffer[6]` reads only one byte.

cards.q: Which cast turns an address into a plain integer?
cards.a:
`reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t>(pointer)`

Turning a pointer into an integer reinterprets its bits, which is `reinterpret_cast`'s job; `static_cast` refuses. `int` is too small to hold a 64-bit address.

cards.q: An `Enemy*` holds `0x5000` and `health` is at offset 12. What address does `enemy->health` read?
cards.a:
`0x500C`

The arrow is "base address plus member offset": 0x5000 + 12 = `0x500C`, since 12 is `0xC` in hex. The offset is in bytes, not in elements.

cards.q: `struct S { char a; int b; char c; };` What is `sizeof(S)`, and why?
cards.a:
12: `a` at 0, padding, `b` at 4, `c` at 8, then trailing padding to a multiple of 4

The `int` needs a 4-aligned offset, so three bytes of padding follow `a`, and the size is padded to a multiple of 4 so arrays of `S` stay aligned. The compiler never reorders members.

cards.q: How can that struct be made smaller?
cards.a:
Put the `int` first: `int b; char a; char c;` gives offsets 0, 4, 5 and size 8

Ordering members from largest to smallest leaves less padding. Adding a member into the trailing padding keeps the size at 12; it uses the waste but does not remove it.

cards.q: Why should a struct not be compared with `memcmp`?
cards.a:
Its padding bytes have unspecified contents, so two structs with equal members can still differ byte for byte

Padding is not part of any member and nothing promises what it holds. Compare the members one by one, or with a defaulted `operator==`.

cards.q: `int x{ 1 }; int* p{ &x }; int** pp{ &p };` What are `*pp` and `**pp`?
cards.a:
`*pp` is `p` (the address of `x`); `**pp` is `x`, 1

Each `*` follows one level: from `pp` to `p`, then from `p` to `x`.

cards.q: Why does a function that creates an object for the caller often take `Thing** out`?
cards.a:
It needs to change the caller's pointer variable, so it needs that variable's address

With `Thing* out` the function gets a copy of the caller's pointer, and changing the copy does nothing for the caller. With `Thing**` it can write `*out = new Thing{}`.

cards.q: In the pointer-to-pointer removal from a linked list, why is the first node not a special case?
cards.a:
`link` points at `head` or at a `next`, and `*link` is updated either way

The trick walks a pointer to the pointer that leads to the current node. Whether that is `head` or some node's `next`, assigning through it unlinks the node the same way.

cards.q: What is `argv[argc]`?
cards.a:
`nullptr`: the array of argument pointers ends with a null pointer

`argv[0]` is usually the program name and `argv[argc - 1]` the last argument. The standard guarantees an extra null pointer at `argv[argc]`.

cards.q: In the chain `base -> 0x00 -> 0x00 -> 0x08 -> 0x10 -> 0x04`, why is the last offset added without a read?
cards.a:
The last step gives the address of the value itself; every earlier step reads a pointer to the next object

Every step but the last lands on a pointer, which is read to reach the next object. The final offset points at the value you want, so you stop with its address.

cards.q: Why must a chain be checked for `nullptr` at every step?
cards.a:
Any object on the path may not exist at that moment

For example, there may be no level loaded yet. Reading through its null pointer would crash; a null check at each read turns that into a clean "not found".

cards.q: Why does the address of `health` change between runs while the chain stays the same?
cards.a:
Objects move, but offsets and the anchoring global are fixed

ASLR and the heap move the objects every run, but the layout of every struct and the position of the first link's global inside the program are fixed when it is built.

cards.q: Where does offset `0x08` in the World step come from?
cards.a:
From the layout: `offsetof(World, players)` after padding

The pointer member `players` needs 8-byte alignment, so after the 4-byte `int tick` there are 4 bytes of padding and `players` sits at offset 8.

cards.q: Why does inserting into the middle of a linked list not depend on its length?
cards.a:
Only the pointers of the neighbouring nodes change; nothing has to move

Once you hold a pointer to the place, linking a node in rewrites two or so pointers. A vector, by contrast, must move every element after the insertion point.

cards.q: Why is walking a linked list usually much slower than walking a vector with the same values?
cards.a:
The nodes are scattered in memory, so almost every step is a cache miss, while a vector is read sequentially

A vector's elements are next to each other, so the processor fetches them in big runs ahead of time. Each list node can be anywhere, so the next one usually has to come from main memory.

cards.q: What does a sentinel node remove from a doubly linked list's code?
cards.a:
The `nullptr` checks and special cases for the first and last nodes

With a sentinel, every real node always has a real `prev` and `next`, so insert and remove are the same few lines everywhere in the list.

cards.q: In an intrusive list, how do you get from a pointer to the embedded links back to the whole object?
cards.a:
Subtract the links member's offset from its address, as `CONTAINING_RECORD` does

The links sit at a fixed offset inside the object, so the object starts that many bytes earlier. A plain cast only works when the links are the first member.

cards.q: What does `int (*f)(double)` declare?
cards.a:
`f`, a pointer to a function that takes a `double` and returns an `int`

The brackets around `*f` make `f` a pointer first; the rest describes what it points at. Without them, `int* f(double)` declares a function returning `int*`.

cards.q: Why do C-style callback APIs take a `void*` context argument?
cards.a:
A function pointer carries no data, so the caller's state goes as a `void*`

The library does not know your type, so it stores an untyped address and hands it back unchanged to your callback, which casts it back to what it really is.

cards.q: What happens, step by step, in a virtual call `unit->attack()`?
cards.a:
Read the vtable pointer from the object, read `attack`'s address from its slot in the table, call that address

Each object of a class with virtual functions holds a hidden pointer to its class's table of function addresses. Calling picks the address from that table at run time.

cards.q: Which lambdas can be passed where a plain function pointer is expected?
cards.a:
Lambdas with no captures

A lambda without captures has no state and converts to a plain function pointer. A capturing lambda carries data, which a function pointer has no room for; use `std::function` or a `void*` context instead.

cards.q: Is it safe for a function to return a `const char*` pointing at the literal `"error"`?
cards.a:
Yes, string literals have static storage and live for the whole program

A string literal is stored with the program's static data, not on the stack, so a pointer to it never dangles. A local `char` array holding the same text would be a different story.

cards.q: When is a `static` local variable initialised?
cards.a:
The first time execution passes its declaration

A static local has static storage but is set up lazily, on the first pass through its declaration; after that it keeps its value between calls until the program ends.

cards.q: A function creates a 4 MB array as a local variable. What is likely to happen?
cards.a:
A stack overflow, because the default stack is 1 MB; use a `std::vector` instead

Each thread's stack is small and fixed, 1 MB by default on Windows. A `std::vector` keeps its elements on the heap, which has room for big buffers.

cards.q: Which storage duration do the elements inside a `std::vector` have?
cards.a:
Dynamic: the vector object can be a local, but its elements are allocated on the heap

The small vector object (a few pointers) lives wherever you declare it. The elements it manages are always on the heap.

cards.q: Does the stack pointer go up or down when a function is called on x64?
cards.a:
Down: the new frame is at lower addresses than the caller's

The x64 stack grows towards lower addresses, so pushing a frame subtracts from the stack pointer and returning adds back.

cards.q: Why might printing through a pointer to a dead local still show the old value?
cards.a:
Returning only moves the stack pointer; the bytes stay until reused

Nothing clears a frame when it is popped. The old value lingers until the next call writes its own frame over that part of the stack, which is why the bug seems to work at first.

cards.q: What is the default stack size of a thread on Windows, and what happens when it runs out?
cards.a:
1 MB, and a stack overflow exception ends the program

Windows reserves 1 MB per thread by default with a guard page at the end. Touching it, by deep recursion or a huge local, raises a stack overflow exception.

cards.q: What does the `/GS` security cookie protect?
cards.a:
The return address, with a checked value placed before it

A random value sits between the locals and the return address and is checked before returning. An overrun that reaches the return address must first overwrite it, so the check catches it.

cards.q: What two things does `new Enemy{...}` do?
cards.a:
Get memory from the allocator, then run `Enemy`'s constructor in it

`new` is allocation plus construction, and `delete` is destruction plus freeing. `malloc` only does the first half.

cards.q: Why does `delete` need no size?
cards.a:
The allocator stores the block's size in a header next to the block

The allocator keeps bookkeeping next to every block it hands out, so given the address it knows how much to release.

cards.q: Writing one int past the end of a heap array often does nothing visible at first. Why does it crash later?
cards.a:
It overwrites the next block's header, and the damage is noticed only when the allocator next uses that header

The overrun lands in the allocator's bookkeeping or a neighbour's data. Nothing checks it at the time of the write, so the crash comes at a later `new` or `delete`.

cards.q: What is wrong with `int* a = new int[8]; delete a;`?
cards.a:
An array allocated with `new[]` must be freed with `delete[]`

The pairs must match exactly: `new` with `delete`, `new[]` with `delete[]`, `malloc` with `free`. A mismatch is undefined behaviour, not merely a leak.

cards.q: Two parts of a program both `delete` the same object. Which rule was broken?
cards.a:
The object had two owners, and every heap object must have exactly one

One owner frees; everyone else only borrows. Two owners means a double free.

cards.q: A function's documentation says "the returned string must be freed with `LocalFree`". Who owns the string?
cards.a:
The caller, who must free it with `LocalFree`

Ownership passes to the caller when the function returns, and memory must go back to the allocator it came from, so `delete` or `free` would be a mismatched free.

cards.q: Destroying a `std::vector<Enemy*>` frees what?
cards.a:
Only the vector's own array of pointers, not the enemies they point at

A container owns its elements, and here the elements are pointers. The enemies themselves need an owner that deletes them.

cards.q: Why should a class that owns raw pointers delete its copy constructor?
cards.a:
The default copy copies the pointers, giving two owners that would both delete the same objects

The compiler's copy duplicates addresses, not objects, so both copies' destructors free the same memory. Deleting the copy (or writing a real one) prevents the double free.

cards.q: Why is a leak in a long-running game more serious than in a short command-line tool?
cards.a:
A game that leaks a little every frame keeps growing for hours until it slows down or runs out of memory

Windows reclaims everything when any program exits, so a short tool barely notices. A leak per frame adds up to gigabytes over a long session.
cards.lessonTitle: Leaks and How to Find Them

cards.q: The leak report shows `{157} normal block`. How do you find the code that allocated it?
cards.a:
Call `_CrtSetBreakAlloc(157)` early in `main` and rerun

157 is the allocation's sequence number, not a line or an address. As long as the program runs the same way, the debugger stops when allocation 157 happens.
cards.lessonTitle: Leaks and How to Find Them

cards.q: A leaked block's data shows `CD CD CD CD`. What does that tell you?
cards.a:
The block was allocated but never written to

The debug heap fills new blocks with `0xCD` ("clean"). Seeing it in a leaked block means nobody ever stored anything there.
cards.lessonTitle: Leaks and How to Find Them

cards.q: Which pair of bugs does AddressSanitizer report at the moment they happen?
cards.a:
Heap buffer overflow and use after free

AddressSanitizer catches overflows (heap, stack and global), use after free, use after return, double free and mismatched `new[]`/`delete`. Races are ThreadSanitizer's job, and uninitialised reads are MemorySanitizer's.
cards.lessonTitle: Leaks and How to Find Them

cards.q: What does C++ guarantee that makes RAII work?
cards.a:
A destructor runs on every way out of its object's scope

C++ has no garbage collector, and it does not pair `new` with `delete` for you. What it does promise is that a scoped object's destructor runs on `return`, `break`, exceptions and falling off the end.

cards.q: Two RAII objects `a` and `b` are created in that order in one scope. Which is destroyed first?
cards.a:
`b`, because destruction runs in reverse order of creation

Locals are destroyed in reverse order, so something created later, which may depend on an earlier object, is cleaned up before it.

cards.q: Why must an RAII class that wraps a `FILE*` do something about copying?
cards.a:
The default copy would copy the pointer, so two objects would both close the same file

The compiler's copy duplicates the pointer, not the open file. Delete the copy operations, or define what a copy means.

cards.q: What is a scope guard's `dismiss()` for?
cards.a:
Cancelling the clean-up action, for commit-or-roll-back code, once the work has succeeded

A guard rolls back if the scope is left early. When everything went well you dismiss it, so the roll-back does not happen.

cards.q: Why can a `std::unique_ptr` not be copied?
cards.a:
It is the sole owner, and a copy would create two owners that both delete the object

Making it move-only puts "exactly one owner" into the type: the compiler refuses any code that would make a second owner.

cards.q: After `auto b = std::move(a);` with `a` a `unique_ptr`, what does `a` hold?
cards.a:
`nullptr`, because ownership moved to `b`

Moving transfers ownership: `b` takes the pointer and `a` is left empty, so only one of them will ever delete the object.

cards.q: What is the difference between `p.reset()` and `p.release()`?
cards.a:
`reset` deletes the object; `release` gives up ownership and returns the pointer

Both leave `p` empty. Calling `release()` and ignoring the result leaks the object, because nobody owns it any more; `reset()` is the one that frees.

cards.q: How do you make a `unique_ptr` that closes a `FILE*` instead of deleting it?
cards.a:
Give it a custom deleter whose `operator()` calls `fclose`

The deleter, given as the second template argument, decides what "free" means. With `fclose` as the deleter, the file is closed on every path out, and there is no second close.

cards.q: When does a `shared_ptr` delete its object?
cards.a:
When the last `shared_ptr` owning it is destroyed or reset

Each owner adds one to the strong count and removes one when it goes; at zero the object is deleted. Weak pointers do not keep it alive.

cards.q: Why is `std::make_shared` better than `shared_ptr<T>(new T)`?
cards.a:
It allocates the object and the control block in one heap block instead of two

Every `shared_ptr` needs a control block for the counts. With `new T` that is a second allocation; `make_shared` puts both in one.

cards.q: Two objects hold `shared_ptr`s to each other. What happens when everything else lets go of them?
cards.a:
Neither count reaches zero, so both leak

Each keeps the other's count at one, forever. Break the cycle with a `weak_ptr` in one direction.

cards.q: How do you use the object a `weak_ptr` refers to?
cards.a:
Call `lock()` and check the `shared_ptr` it returns

A `weak_ptr` cannot be dereferenced, because the object might already be gone. `lock()` returns an empty `shared_ptr` if it is, or a temporary owner if it is alive.

cards.q: What does a `std::span` hold?
cards.a:
A pointer to the first element and the number of elements

A span is just a pointer and a length. It owns nothing and copies nothing.

cards.q: Why is a `std::span` passed by value rather than by reference?
cards.a:
It is just a pointer and a size, so copying it is cheap

A span is about 16 bytes. Copying it copies two small values, not the data, so a reference to it would only add an extra level of indirection.

cards.q: Why must you not pass a `string_view`'s `data()` to a C function expecting a C string?
cards.a:
A `string_view` need not be followed by a zero byte, so the function would read past its end

A view can be a slice out of the middle of a longer string, so the byte after its last character can be anything. C functions read until they find a zero.

cards.q: A span views a vector, then elements are pushed onto the vector. What can go wrong?
cards.a:
The vector may move its elements to a new block, leaving the span pointing at freed memory

A view does not know when what it views changes. If `push_back` reallocates, the span's pointer dangles, the same bug as a raw pointer into a vector.

cards.q: What goes wrong when a class owning a raw `new[]` array uses the default copy constructor?
cards.a:
Both objects hold the same pointer, so both destructors delete the same array

The default copy is a shallow copy of the members, so the pointer is duplicated, not the array. That is a double delete, and a change through one is seen by the other.
cards.lessonTitle: Copy and Move for Owning Types

cards.q: What must a move constructor do to the object it moved from?
cards.a:
Leave it empty, with its pointer set to `nullptr`

The moved-from object must stay valid but own nothing, so its destructor frees nothing. If it kept the pointer, both destructors would free it; if the move freed it, the new object would dangle.
cards.lessonTitle: Copy and Move for Owning Types

cards.q: Why should a move constructor be `noexcept`?
cards.a:
`std::vector` only moves elements when growing if the move cannot throw; otherwise it copies them

To keep its strong exception guarantee, a growing vector falls back to copying unless the move is marked `noexcept`.
cards.lessonTitle: Copy and Move for Owning Types

cards.q: What is the rule of zero?
cards.a:
If every member manages its own resource, the class needs no destructor and no copy or move functions of its own

Let members like `std::vector`, `std::string` and `std::unique_ptr` do the owning, and the compiler-generated functions are already right. A class that owns a raw pointer itself still needs the rule of five.
cards.lessonTitle: Copy and Move for Owning Types

cards.q: Why does an allocator split a large free block?
cards.a:
So a small request does not use up the whole block

Without splitting, a 16-byte request could swallow a 4 KB free block. Splitting gives the request what it asked for and keeps the rest available as a smaller free block.

cards.q: What is fragmentation?
cards.a:
Free memory scattered in small blocks between used ones

A large request can then fail although enough memory is free in total. A leak is memory nobody frees; fragmentation is free memory in the wrong shape, and joining neighbouring free blocks fights it.

cards.q: Where are the `next` pointers of a free list stored?
cards.a:
Inside the free blocks themselves, since their memory is not in use

A free block's bytes are not being used for anything, so the allocator stores its bookkeeping there and needs no extra memory.

cards.q: What does `(value + 15) & ~15` do?
cards.a:
Rounds `value` up to the next multiple of 16

Adding 15 pushes any value that is not already a multiple of 16 past the next one, and `& ~15` clears the low 4 bits to land on it. A value that is already a multiple stays the same.

cards.q: What does allocating from an arena cost?
cards.a:
Rounding the offset up for alignment, one comparison against the end, and one addition

An arena only moves one offset forward, which is why it is the fastest allocator there is. It keeps no headers and no free list.

cards.q: Why is an arena a good fit for per-frame memory in a game?
cards.a:
Everything from a frame dies together, so one reset frees it

When lifetimes all end together, freeing each object separately is wasted work. Resetting the offset to zero releases the whole frame's memory at once.

cards.q: What does rewinding to a marker free?
cards.a:
Everything allocated after the marker was taken; earlier allocations stay

A marker is a saved offset. Moving the offset back to it releases what came after, so a function can use scratch memory and give it all back on return.

cards.q: Why should objects in an arena be trivially destructible?
cards.a:
`reset` does not call destructors, so anything that owns other resources would leak them

An arena just forgets its memory. A `std::string` or `std::vector` inside would never free its own heap block.

cards.q: Why does a pool allocator have no fragmentation?
cards.a:
Every block is the same size, so any free block satisfies any request

Fragmentation is a free block of the wrong size. In a pool there is only one size, so every free block always fits.

cards.q: Where does the pool keep the list of free blocks?
cards.a:
In the free blocks themselves, as a linked list

Each free block's first bytes hold the `next` pointer. That memory is unused anyway, so the list costs nothing extra. A bitmap would work too, but that is not how this pool is built.

cards.q: Why must each block be at least `sizeof(void*)` bytes?
cards.a:
A free block has to hold the pointer to the next free block

The free list lives inside the free blocks, so each one must be big enough to hold an 8-byte pointer in a 64-bit program.

cards.q: Why do use-after-free bugs on pooled objects show up quickly?
cards.a:
The free-list pointer overwrites it, and it is reused next

Pools reuse in LIFO order: the block just freed is the next one allocated, and its first bytes are overwritten at once by the free-list pointer. The stale pointer soon sees another object's data.

cards.q: For the address `0x12345`, what are the page number and the offset with 4 KB pages?
cards.a:
Page `0x12`, offset `0x345`

A 4 KB page is `0x1000` bytes, so the low 12 bits (3 hex digits) are the offset and the rest is the page number.

cards.q: What is the difference between reserving and committing memory?
cards.a:
Reserving sets aside addresses; committing puts memory behind them

Reserved pages have nothing behind them, so they fault when touched. Committing backs them with memory, which is what makes them usable.

cards.q: Why does every null pointer dereference fault immediately on Windows?
cards.a:
The lowest 64 KB of the address space is never mapped, so any address near 0 has no translation

There is no special hardware rule. Windows simply never maps those pages, so `nullptr` and small offsets from it always fault.

cards.q: How does page heap catch a buffer overrun at the exact instruction?
cards.a:
It puts each allocation just before an inaccessible page

Each allocation ends at the end of a page with an inaccessible page after it, so the first byte past the end faults. Guard bytes, by contrast, only show the damage when the block is freed.

cards.q: A crash reports reading address `0xDDDDDDDDDDDDDDE5`. What happened?
cards.a:
A pointer was read out of freed heap memory (the `DD` fill), then a member at offset 8 was accessed

`0xDD...DD + 8 = 0xDD...E5`. The pointer itself came from a deleted object, a use after free one level removed. Uninitialised stack memory is filled with `0xCC` instead.
cards.lessonTitle: A Field Guide to Memory Bugs

cards.q: Something overwrites a struct's field and you cannot see where. Which debugger feature finds the culprit?
cards.a:
A data breakpoint on the field's address, which stops at the instruction that writes to it

A data breakpoint watches the memory, not a line of code, so it catches the write wherever it comes from, even through a stray pointer.
cards.lessonTitle: A Field Guide to Memory Bugs

cards.q: What do AddressSanitizer, page heap and the debug heap's fill patterns have in common?
cards.a:
They make a memory bug fail at, or near, the moment of the mistake instead of later

Memory bugs are hard because the crash comes far from the cause. These tools shrink that distance so the debugger stops close to the bug.
cards.lessonTitle: A Field Guide to Memory Bugs

cards.q: A program works in a Debug build but crashes in Release. Which pair of causes is likely?
cards.a:
An uninitialised variable and undefined behaviour that the optimiser exploited

Debug builds fill and keep memory differently and do not optimise, so uninitialised reads, aliasing violations and other undefined behaviour often only bite in Release. The other pairs would fail in both builds, or not crash at all.
cards.lessonTitle: A Field Guide to Memory Bugs
